lessons.title: Two minutes in the box
lessons.objective: Name the common minor penalties and what happens after one.

payload.prompt: Match the foul to a two-minute minor penalty.

pairs.definition: Using the stick to hold or impede an opponent; a two-minute minor.
Bringing someone down with stick or leg; a two-minute minor.
Stick contact above the shoulders; a minor or double minor if blood.

explanation.summary: These are the most common minor penalties you'll hear called all night long.
explanation.sayThisLine: Hooking, tripping, high stick: these three you'll see constantly.

payload.prompt: What happens when a player is called for a two-minute minor?

options.text: They sit in the penalty box; the other team gets a man advantage (power play)
They are ejected from the game
The team pays a fine and keeps playing 5-on-5

explanation.correct: Exactly. A minor sends the player to the sin bin for two minutes. Meanwhile, the other team usually plays 5-on-4. The penalty ends early if the power-play team scores.
explanation.incorrect: A two-minute minor means the player sits in the penalty box while the opposing team has a power play (one extra skater). Nobody is ejected, and there's no fine on the scoreboard; the team just plays a skater short.

payload.prompt: Match three more common minors to what causes them.

pairs.definition: Swinging the stick at an opponent or his stick; a minor, or a major if someone is hurt.
Shoving, punching or scrapping without a full fight; usually a two-minute minor.
Stalling on purpose, such as sending the puck over the glass from your own zone; a two-minute minor.

explanation.summary: Slashing, roughing and delay of game are everyday minors too. Hearing one in a broadcast usually means a two-minute power play is next.

payload.prompt: A two-minute minor penalty ends as soon as the power-play team scores. True or false?

scene.alt: A player sits in the penalty box while the opposing team scores on the power play, and the shorthanded player is waved out.

explanation.correct: True. When the power-play team scores, the minor ends and the penalized player comes out of the box. That's why a power-play goal cuts the power play short.
explanation.incorrect: A goal by the team on the power play does end a minor. The penalized player leaves the box, and play goes back to full strength unless other penalties are running.

payload.question: What just happened?

options.text: Number 7 used their stick to hold an opponent
Number 7 is going to the penalty box for two minutes
The other team gets a power play
Number 7 will be ejected if they do it again

payload.translation: The referee called hooking on number 7, meaning they used their stick to hold or impede an opponent. They go to the box for two minutes while the other team gets a man advantage.

followUps.line: How long was that power play?
followUps.why: Tests if you understand it ends early with a goal.

followUps.line: Could the high stick also be a minor?
followUps.why: Shows you know different infractions have different penalties.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Refs call hooking and tripping constantly; you'll get used to them quickly.

lessons.title: Stick fouls: high stick, holding, interference
lessons.objective: Distinguish the stick and contact minors.

payload.prompt: Match the stick foul to its description.

pairs.definition: The stick makes contact above the shoulders; a minor, or a double minor if it draws blood.
Using hands or arms to grab or hold an opponent; a two-minute minor.
Hitting or blocking a player who doesn't have the puck; a two-minute minor.

explanation.summary: High stick is a stick foul; holding and interference are about how you treat the other player's body. All three usually mean two minutes.
explanation.sayThisLine: That's interference; he didn't have the puck.

payload.prompt: A high stick that draws blood is a four-minute double minor. True or false?

scene.alt: A player's stick makes contact with an opponent's face and blood is visible.

explanation.correct: True. A high stick that draws blood is a double minor: two consecutive two-minute minors, four minutes total. If the power-play team scores in the first two, only the first minor ends and the second begins.
explanation.incorrect: A high stick that draws blood is a double minor, served as two back-to-back two-minute minors. A power-play goal in the first two minutes ends that minor only; the second still runs.

payload.prompt: Which of these is holding?

options.text: Wrapping your arms around an opponent to stop him skating
A clean shoulder check on the player with the puck
Lifting an opponent's stick to take the puck

explanation.correct: Right. Holding is grabbing an opponent with your hands or arms to keep him from moving. A clean check and a stick lift are both legal.
explanation.incorrect: Holding means grabbing or clutching an opponent to stop him skating. A clean body check and a stick lift are legal; holding is a two-minute minor.

payload.prompt: Complete the double minor rule.
payload.template: A double minor is {{duration}} minutes of penalties. If the power-play team scores in the first two, the first minor ends and the second {{happens}}.

explanation.correct: Exactly. A double minor is two back-to-back minors. A power-play goal ends the one that's running, then the second starts.
explanation.incorrect: A double minor is four minutes, served as two consecutive two-minute minors. A goal during the first two ends that minor only; the second still has to be served.

statement.speaker: Analyst
statement.text: That's holding. You can't wrap a guy up like that.

payload.question: What did the player do?

options.text: He grabbed an opponent with his hands or arms
He'll probably serve a two-minute minor
His team may now be shorthanded
He made a legal check

payload.translation: Holding means grabbing or clutching an opponent to stop him. It isn't a legal check; it's normally a two-minute minor.

followUps.why: Shows you know they're related but separate calls.

followUps.line: Did they score on the power play?
followUps.why: Moves the chat to what happened next.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Holding and interference are cousins, so it's fine to ask which one the ref called.

lessons.title: Boarding, charging, cross-checking
lessons.objective: Recognize the dangerous fouls that draw majors.

payload.prompt: A major penalty is five minutes in the box. True or false?

scene.alt: A player sits in the penalty box with an angry expression; the scoreboard shows a five-minute penalty timer.

explanation.correct: True. A major is five minutes, served in full, even if the power-play team scores. Majors go to serious fouls, like fighting or a dangerous hit that hurts someone.
explanation.incorrect: A major is five minutes. Unlike a minor, a power-play goal does not end it; it runs its full duration. The worst ones can also lead to a league suspension.

payload.prompt: What is boarding?

options.text: Driving an opponent into the boards with force; can be a minor or major depending on how hard
Checking an opponent who is standing on the boards
Using the boards to push yourself away from an opponent

explanation.correct: Exactly. Boarding is a dangerous hit into the boards. A lesser boarding is a two-minute minor; a dangerous one, especially with an injury, is a five-minute major with a game misconduct, and may draw a suspension from the Department of Player Safety.
explanation.incorrect: Boarding means hitting a defenseless opponent hard into the boards. It's called because the boards make the hit dangerous, and the severity depends on the force and any injury.

payload.prompt: Match the dangerous foul to its description.

pairs.definition: Driving an opponent forcefully into the boards; a minor or major depending on severity.
Skating or jumping into an opponent with extra momentum; a minor or major depending on force.
Hitting an opponent with the shaft of the stick, both hands on it; usually a minor, a major if it injures.

explanation.summary: Each of these starts as a minor, and the referee moves it up to a major when the force or injury is serious. They exist to protect players.
explanation.sayThisLine: That's a cross-check. Two minutes, or five if someone's hurt.

payload.prompt: Complete the major penalty rule.
payload.template: A minor lasts {{minor}} minutes; a major lasts {{major}} and ignores power-play goals.

explanation.correct: Right. A minor is two minutes and ends early on a power-play goal. A major is five minutes, always served in full.
explanation.incorrect: A minor is two minutes; a major is five. Only a minor ends early on a power-play goal, while a major runs its full duration because it's for a more serious foul.

statement.speaker: Analyst
statement.text: That was boarding on the replay. He drove him into the boards pretty hard; five minutes and probably in the Department of Player Safety's office tomorrow.

payload.question: What is the analyst saying?

options.text: The player made a dangerous hit into the boards
It could be reviewed for a suspension
It's a five-minute major penalty
The player will be ejected from the game

payload.translation: Boarding is aggressively driving an opponent into the boards. A five-minute major is on the ice; a suspension comes later if the league reviews it.

followUps.line: Will he be back for the next game?
followUps.why: Tests if you know majors and suspensions are separate.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Majors and suspensions are different; a major is on the ice, a suspension comes from the league.

lessons.title: Misconducts, ejections and fights
lessons.objective: Explain game and match penalties and what a fighting major is.

payload.prompt: Complete the misconduct penalty rule.
payload.template: A game misconduct ejects a player for {{duration}}. By itself, it leaves his team at {{strength}}.

explanation.correct: Right. A game misconduct sends the player to the dressing room for the night, but by itself it costs his team no skaters. Any power play comes from a separate minor or major that came with it.
explanation.incorrect: A game misconduct is an ejection for the rest of the game, not a season-long ban (that's a suspension). On its own, the team isn't shorthanded.

payload.prompt: What happens if two players start fighting?

options.text: Each gets a five-minute major, and the teams stay at full strength
Both players are ejected and each team plays a skater short
Each gets a two-minute minor and the play goes 4-on-4

explanation.correct: Exactly. Fighting majors are five minutes each. They offset, so neither team goes shorthanded and it stays 5-on-5.
explanation.incorrect: In the NHL a fight costs each fighter a five-minute major. Because both teams get one, they cancel out and play continues at full strength. Fights are much rarer than they used to be.

payload.prompt: Match the ejection type to its meaning.

pairs.definition: Ejection for the rest of the game; on its own, the team isn't shorthanded.
Ejection for a deliberate attempt to injure; the team plays five minutes shorthanded.
Five minutes for each fighter; the majors offset, so both teams stay at full strength.

explanation.summary: These are the serious consequences: ejection, extra time shorthanded and possible league discipline. The NHL allows a fight to play out as a major; the PWHL and international hockey treat fighting as a more serious offense.
explanation.sayThisLine: Game misconduct, he's done for the night.

payload.prompt: After a fight, both teams play 4-on-4 for five minutes. True or false?

scene.alt: Two players are escorted to opposite penalty boxes after fighting.

explanation.correct: False. Matching fighting majors offset, so both teams keep five skaters. Neither side gets a power play.
explanation.incorrect: It stays 5-on-5. The two majors cancel each other out, which is why a fight on its own doesn't create a power play.

payload.question: What just happened?

options.text: Number 18 is ejected from the game
The team does not go shorthanded
The league can still review it for further discipline
A goal will bring him back

payload.translation: A game misconduct is an ejection. The player leaves for the night, and on its own the team stays at full strength. The league can still look at it for a suspension.

followUps.line: Is he done for the season or just tonight?
followUps.why: Tests if you know a misconduct is just an ejection, separate from suspension.

followUps.line: What's the difference between a misconduct and a fighting major?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: A misconduct means ejection; the Department of Player Safety decides about suspension later.

lessons.title: The power play, in one sentence
lessons.objective: Explain what a man advantage is and how it ends.

payload.prompt: What is a power play in one sentence?

options.text: One team has a man advantage because the other is serving a penalty
A team scores a goal while playing fast
Two teams play 5-on-5 after a stoppage

explanation.correct: Exactly. A power play is when you have more skaters than the other team because they have a player in the box. A 5-on-4 is the most common.
explanation.incorrect: A power play is a man-advantage situation: your team has more skaters on the ice because the other team is serving a penalty. A minor ends when its time runs out or when the team with the advantage scores.

payload.prompt: How does a minor-penalty power play end?
payload.template: A minor-penalty power play lasts {{time}} minutes, or less if the {{who}} team scores.

explanation.correct: Right. A minor runs two minutes, and a goal by the team with the advantage ends it early.
explanation.incorrect: A minor power play is two minutes long. It ends early only when the team with the extra skater scores; a shorthanded goal doesn't end it.

payload.prompt: A 5-on-4 power play happens most often because of what?

options.text: A two-minute minor penalty on the other team
A five-minute major penalty on the other team
The opponent pulled their goalie

explanation.correct: Correct. A two-minute minor gives you a 5-on-4. A five-minute major also does, but majors are rarer. A 5-on-3 is the bigger advantage (two penalties at once).
explanation.incorrect: A 5-on-4 most often comes from a two-minute minor. A major can also create one, but minors are far more frequent. A pulled goalie creates an extra attacker, not a power play.

statement.speaker: Announcer
statement.text: And that's a power-play goal! One-one!

payload.question: What does that mean?

options.text: The team scored while on the power play
The score is now tied at one goal each
If it was a minor, the penalty is now over
The game just went to overtime

payload.translation: A power-play goal means the team with the man advantage scored. If the penalty was a minor, it ends right away and play goes back to even strength.

followUps.line: Does a power-play goal count differently than a regular goal?
followUps.why: Shows you know it's worth one goal, same as any other.
Shows you know PP% is goals ÷ power plays.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Power-play goals are huge momentum shifts; fans love them because they show special-teams execution.

lessons.title: Surviving a penalty kill
lessons.objective: Describe what the shorthanded team is trying to do.

payload.prompt: When a shorthanded team scores while on the penalty kill, what is it called?

options.text: A shorthanded goal
An even-strength goal
A defensive goal

explanation.correct: Right. A shorthanded goal (or 'shorty') is when the team down a man scores. Fans love them because they flip the momentum instantly. The penalty still runs, though.
explanation.incorrect: A shorthanded goal happens when the penalized team scores while defending. It's rare and exciting, and the penalty keeps running (only a power-play goal ends a minor).

payload.prompt: Match the penalty-kill strategy to what it does.

pairs.definition: Four players form a tight box to protect the slot and force perimeter shots; a passive strategy.
The shorthanded team pressures the puck carrier to force turnovers; a risky but potentially rewarding strategy.
Get the puck out of your zone and run out the clock; the most basic goal of the penalty kill.

explanation.summary: A penalty kill is a defensive job: protect the slot, clear the puck, and run out the penalty time. A goal is a bonus.
explanation.sayThisLine: They run a box on the penalty kill: solid, predictable.

payload.prompt: A successful penalty kill means the shorthanded team did not allow a goal. True or false?

scene.alt: The clock shows the penalty time expired and the scoreboard has not changed.

explanation.correct: True. A kill means you got through the penalty without giving up a goal. You don't need to score (though a shorty is incredible); you just need to survive.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, a penalty kill means the penalized team survived without allowing the power-play team to score. A shorty is better than that.

statement.speaker: Coach
statement.text: Our penalty kill is 82 percent. Top five in the league. That's winning defense.

payload.question: What is she saying?

options.text: The team kills 82 out of every 100 penalties
This is a key stat for the team's success
The penalty kill is a defensive unit that prevents power-play goals
The team has not allowed a goal in the last 82 minutes

payload.translation: Penalty kill percentage (PK%) is the share of penalties killed without allowing a goal. 82% means 82 out of every 100 power plays are stopped. A strong penalty kill is crucial.

followUps.line: What's a good penalty kill percentage?
followUps.why: Tests if you know ~80% is average.

followUps.line: How does this compare to the power play?
followUps.why: Shows you understand PK% and PP% are related stats.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Killing penalties is a specialist job; it's fine to ask who their best penalty killers are.

payload.prompt: Order these manpower situations from most to least advantageous for the team on the power play.

items.why: The biggest advantage: five skaters against three, until the first penalty ends.
The most common power play: one extra skater for two minutes.
No power play at all: even strength with fewer skaters, so no advantage for either side.

explanation.correct: Right. 5-on-3 is the best advantage, then 5-on-4, then 4-on-4 (no power play).
explanation.incorrect: A 5-on-3 is the most lethal. A 5-on-4 is standard. A 4-on-4 is no power play; just even strength with fewer skaters.

payload.prompt: When does a 5-on-3 happen?

options.text: Two players on the same team are in the penalty box at the same time (two minors)
One team has a minor and the other gets a major
The team on the power play pulls its goalie

explanation.correct: Exactly. A 5-on-3 is when one team has two penalties running at the same time, so the other side has five skaters against three. It's the biggest advantage in the game.
explanation.incorrect: A 5-on-3 means the shorthanded team has two players in the box at once. A minor against one team and a major against the other cancel out, so that doesn't do it.

payload.prompt: Complete the 4-on-4 rule.
payload.template: Matching minors mean {{result}} hockey, so neither team gets a {{what}}, and only {{total}} skaters are on the ice.

explanation.correct: Right. When both teams get a minor at the same time, each plays a skater short, so it's 4-on-4 with eight skaters and no power play. The extra ice often opens the game up.
explanation.incorrect: Matching minors cancel each other out as an advantage, but each team still loses a skater, so play is 4-on-4 with eight skaters in total.

payload.prompt: A 5-on-3 becomes a 5-on-4 when the first penalty runs out. True or false?

scene.alt: The scoreboard shows two penalty timers, one expiring before the other.

explanation.correct: True. As soon as the earlier penalty ends, one player returns and the power play continues as a 5-on-4 until the second penalty ends. The 5-on-3 window is short, so teams try to score in it.
explanation.incorrect: The 5-on-3 lasts only until the first of the two penalties ends. Then one player returns and it's a regular 5-on-4 for whatever time is left on the other.

lessons.title: Penalty shots and embellishment
lessons.objective: Recognize a penalty shot and a dive.

payload.prompt: When is a penalty shot awarded?

options.text: When a player is fouled from behind on a clear breakaway, preventing a goal-scoring chance
When a team gets five penalties in one period
When a player shoots and misses the net

explanation.correct: Right. A penalty shot is one-on-one against the goalie: the fouled player starts at center ice and tries to score with no defenders. It gives back the scoring chance the foul took away.
explanation.incorrect: A penalty shot is awarded when a player on a clear breakaway is fouled from behind. He gets a one-on-one try against the goalie, starting from center ice. Shooting and missing, or a pile of penalties, doesn't earn one.

payload.prompt: Match the scoring opportunity to its description.

pairs.definition: A one-on-one against the goalie awarded for a foul on a breakaway; starts from center ice.
A team advantage because the opponent has a player in the box; more attackers than defenders.
A best-of-three one-on-one competition to break a tie after 3-on-3 overtime (not used in NHL playoffs).

explanation.summary: A penalty shot is rare and dramatic. It's not a power play; it's a single chance, one shooter, one goalie. The shootout borrows that one-on-one format.
explanation.sayThisLine: Penalty shot! He was fouled on the breakaway.

payload.prompt: Embellishment is when a player exaggerates or fakes a foul to draw a penalty. True or false?

scene.alt: A player falls dramatically after minimal contact from an opponent.

explanation.correct: True. Embellishment (or 'diving') is when a player sells a foul that didn't happen, exaggerates, or falls theatrically. Referees can call it on the diver, and the league can fine repeat offenders.
explanation.incorrect: Embellishment is faking or exaggerating contact to draw a penalty. The referee can call a two-minute minor on the diver, which takes away the power play he hoped to earn.

statement.speaker: Analyst
statement.text: That was a dive. He barely got touched and threw himself on the ice. Two minutes for embellishment.

payload.question: What did the player do?

options.text: They exaggerated or faked a foul
They got caught embellishing and drew a penalty against themselves
The contact was minimal but they sold it theatrically
They were rightfully awarded a penalty shot

payload.translation: Embellishment is selling a foul that didn't happen. If the ref catches the diver, they call embellishment on that player (two minutes). Fans dislike diving.

followUps.line: Does he get a penalty shot if he's caught diving?
followUps.why: Tests if you know embellishment is a penalty against the diver, not a reward.

followUps.line: How often do refs call embellishment?
followUps.why: Shows you know it's a judgment call, and that fans argue about it.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Diving is one of the most debated things in hockey; fans and refs disagree on when it's called.
